title: Symmetric Bead Strand
story: A jewellery maker designs bracelets in a web app. Each bead is stored as a node holding a color code, linked to the next bead on the strand. The app can only walk the strand forwards from the clasp.

Some customers want a symmetric bracelet: it looks the same whether you start reading from the clasp or from the other end. Before an order is accepted, the app checks the strand, and the device it runs on is short on memory, so it should not copy the strand.
task: Write isSymmetric(head). Return true if the sequence of values in the linked list reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise false.
An empty strand and a single bead both count as symmetric. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. You may change the links while you work.

examples.explanation: Read from either end you get 3, 7, 5, 7, 3. The middle bead, 5, pairs with itself.
The middle two beads match, but the ends are 3 and 4. Read backwards the strand is 4, 7, 7, 3, which is different.

hints: In an array you would compare the first value with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. What stops you from doing that on this strand?
You cannot walk backwards from the far end. But what if the second half of the strand pointed the other way? Then you could walk inwards from both ends at once.
You need two tools you may already know: finding the middle with a slow and a fast pointer, and reversing a list in place.

Find the middle with slow/fast pointers. Reverse the list from slow onward. Now walk one pointer from head and one from the reversed half's head, comparing values, until the reversed half runs out. Any mismatch means false.
bruteForce: Copy every color code into an array, then check it with two indexes moving in from both ends. Or push every value on a stack and compare while popping.
Both take O(n) time, which is fine, but they also need O(n) extra memory: a full copy of the strand. The task asks for O(1) extra memory, which means working on the links themselves.

walkthrough: The array check compares pairs from the outside in. A singly linked list cannot walk backwards, so make the second half walk backwards: reverse it in place, then compare from both ends.
• Find the middle. slow/fast go 3/3, then 7/5, then 5/3. fast.next is null, so slow stops on 5.
• Reverse from 5 onward. The second half was 5 → 7 → 3 and becomes 3 → 7 → 5. The first half still runs 3 → 7 → 5, because 7 still points to 5.
• Compare: left 3 vs right 3, left 7 vs right 7, left 5 vs right 5. The reversed half ends. Every pair matched, so return true.

Loop on right, the reversed half, not on left. For an odd length the middle node belongs to both halves and is compared with itself, which is harmless. In real code you would reverse the second half back afterwards so the caller gets the strand unchanged; it is the same reversal loop again.
solution.timeWhy: Three passes, each over at most the whole list.
solution.spaceWhy: Only a few pointers; the reversal reuses the existing nodes.
solution.takeaway: Big linked list problems are often small ones combined. Here: fast/slow pointers to find the middle, in-place reversal, then two pointers walking towards each other. Learn each piece well and you can snap them together.
